analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health service giving free comprehensive health care to everyone in the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action in the House and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995; its sole sponsor drew no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a United States Health Service, an independent government agency run by elected and appointed health boards, that provides comprehensive medical care free of charge to every person in the country. Care would be delivered by salaried government health workers through government health centers, district hospitals, and regional medical facilities. The system would be financed by additional income taxes on individuals and corporations, with the federal Medicare and Medicaid programs, federal employee health insurance, and existing employer health obligations repealed or voided.
analysis.who_benefits: Every individual in the United States would be entitled to comprehensive health care without charge, including the uninsured, people with preexisting conditions, and low-income, rural, and inner-city residents whose needs the bill's findings say the existing system fails. Workers would earn paid time off for medical care, women would be entitled to a full range of reproductive services without coercion, and health workers would be guaranteed salaried government jobs with student loans repaid by the Service.

how_it_helps.text: All individuals in the United States would be eligible for comprehensive health care and supplemental services without charge, without discrimination, delivered through Service facilities.

Every community would get a comprehensive health center, every district a general hospital, and every region a specialized medical facility, with priority attention to underserved inner-city and rural areas.
The bill adds paid health leave to the Fair Labor Standards Act, entitling workers to one hour of paid leave for every 35 hours worked when they or a dependent need health care.

Reproductive services including contraception, pregnancy testing, prenatal care, and abortion would be provided without coercion or harassment and confidentially, and patients would hold an enumerated set of basic health rights enforceable through a grievance and legal-aid system.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and corporations would pay additional income taxes, the tax exclusion for employer-paid health premiums would end, and the Medicare payroll tax would be repealed and folded into the new system. Private health insurers would lose the market the new system replaces, private hospitals and physician practices would be phased out of delivering care in Service facilities, and drug and supply makers would sell into a government formulary and purchasing system that could itself manufacture drugs. Current employer obligations to pay for employees' health care would be voided.

drawbacks.text: Three years after the system took effect, health boards could not let their facilities be used for private delivery of care, and Service employees could not practice privately, so patients would lose the option to pay out of pocket for care outside the government system.

The financing shift is large: new income taxes on individuals and corporations, an end to the employer health insurance tax exclusion, repeal of the Medicare hospital insurance tax, and elimination of employer health obligations and workers' compensation health coverage, all flowing into one new trust fund.
The government would control a national drug formulary, purchase and distribute drugs and medical supplies, and could establish and operate its own drug manufacturing facilities.

Students at the Service's health team schools would have to agree to work for the Service for at least two years or the Service could recover damages, and Service employees would be subject to federal law provisions on striking, limiting their ability to walk off the job.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The promised benefit is the largest available in health policy: free, comprehensive care for every person, ending unpaid medical bills, insurance denials, and coverage gaps. The costs the bill itself acknowledges are equally large: a near-total government takeover of care delivery with a ban on private practice, major new taxes, and a government monopoly on the drug formulary and purchasing. Even supporters of single-payer reform at the time generally proposed less sweeping designs that preserved private providers; this bill took the most maximalist version, and it was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to nine House committees and a string of subcommittees in mid-1993, but no committee ever voted on it and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Ronald Dellums introduced the United States Health Service Act on May 11, 1993.

The bill was referred jointly to nine House committees: Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, Banking Finance and Urban Affairs, District of Columbia, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Post Office and Civil Service, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means.

Between May 18 and July 16, 1993, the bill was referred to nine subcommittees across those committees, with an executive comment requested from the Department of Defense; the action history shows no markup, hearing vote, or floor action after that.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1995, with the bill never reported out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, private hospitals and physician practices, and pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill died: the payment and delivery system it would have replaced stayed in place. The Democratic majority's broader 1993-94 health reform effort, which failed on its own terms, absorbed the policy window instead.

for.name: Rep. Ronald V. Dellums
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 11, 1993; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill; no subcommittee or the full committee ever reported it or scheduled a vote.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill, which contained all of its tax and financing provisions; the committee never acted on it.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Pursued the administration's own managed-competition health plan in 1993-94, making comprehensive single-payer legislation a lower priority for congressional Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors from either party, while the Democratic majority pursued the Clinton administration's own health plan instead.

industries.note: A free universal system would eliminate most of the market for private health coverage, and the bill repeals federal employee health insurance and Medicare and Medicaid provisions that insurers participate in. Insurers would also be barred from governing the new system. Their interest in keeping the current payment system ran against the bill's promise of free care for all.

Care would be delivered by salaried government health workers through Service-built facilities, and three years in, private delivery in those facilities and private practice by Service employees would be prohibited. Private providers' revenue from billed care would be replaced by salaries, which the industry opposed in favor of preserving private billing.

A national formulary would decide which drugs and devices are covered, regional boards would purchase and distribute them, and the National Board could open its own manufacturing facilities, cutting into makers' pricing power. Guaranteed volume under a single purchaser would be offset by government-set coverage and prices.

Existing employer obligations to pay for current and former employees' health care would be voided, but employers would face new taxes and would have to fund a health facility in or near each workplace. Gains and losses for employers genuinely pull in opposite directions.
